claim: A finite automaton is always in one of its states, drawn as circles, and switches from state to state as it reads the string; the numbers in the circles are only labels.
quote: A finite automaton is always in one of its states, represented in the diagram by circles. (The numbers inside the circles are labels to make this discussion easier; they are not part of the machine's operation.) As it reads the string, it switches from state to state.

claim: Start states are drawn with a lone arrowhead pointing at them, and matching (accepting) states are drawn as a double circle.
quote: Start states are depicted with lone arrowheads pointing at them, and matching states are drawn as a double circle.

claim: A finite automaton reads its input one character at a time, following the arrow for each input character to move from state to state.
quote: The machine reads an input string one character at a time, following arrows corresponding to the input to move from state to state.

claim: A finite automaton matches if it ends in a matching state, and stops early if at some point there is no arrow for the current input character.
quote: If the machine ends in a non-matching state, it does not match the string. If, at any point during the machine's execution, there is no arrow for it to follow corresponding to the current input character, the machine stops executing early.

claim: A deterministic finite automaton is one in which, in any state, each possible input letter leads to at most one new state.
quote: The machine we have been considering is called a deterministic finite automaton (DFA), because in any state, each possible input letter leads to at most one new state.

claim: When a machine has several possible next states, it cannot peek ahead to know which is right, and a nondeterministic finite automaton is one allowed to always guess correctly.
quote: Since the machine cannot peek ahead to see the rest of the string, it has no way to know which is the correct decision. In this situation, it turns out to be interesting to let the machine always guess correctly. Such machines are called non-deterministic finite automata (NFAs or NDFAs).

claim: An NFA may, at any time, follow an unlabeled (empty) arrow without reading any input.
quote: An NFA can, at any time, choose to follow an unlabeled arrow without reading any input.

claim: Unlabeled arrows can always be removed from an NFA or avoided when building it, but they make the NFA easier to read and understand.
quote: it is always possible to remove the unlabeled arrows, and it is also always possible to generate the NFA without the unlabeled arrows in the first place. Having the unlabeled arrows makes the NFA easier for us to read and understand

claim: Guessing can be simulated by letting the machine be in multiple states at once and, for each letter, advancing all the states along all the arrows that match it.
quote: In this approach, the simulation allows the machine to be in multiple states at once. To process each letter, it advances all the states along all the arrows that match the letter.

claim: In the multiple-state simulation the machine starts in the start state together with all states reachable from it by unlabeled arrows.
quote: The machine starts in the start state and all the states reachable from the start state by unlabeled arrows.

locator: Caching the NFA to build a DFA
claim: Any NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA in which each DFA state corresponds to a list of NFA states.
quote: Any NFA can be converted into an equivalent DFA in which each DFA state corresponds to a list of NFA states.
